data.title: DOJ gives California counties 48 hours to help identify suspected noncitizen voters
data.description:
DOJ orders some California counties to verify ballots in 48 hours

SAFIYAH RIDDLE
Updated Sat, October 24, 2026 at 1:29 AM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Los Angeles (AP) — Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Department of Justice said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press.

The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Donald Trump's Department of Justice, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

Earlier this month, the federal government targeted Los Angeles County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of roughly 20,000 people who are "likely" noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday.

Advertisement

The Trump administration asked the 9th Circuit court of appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday.

Now, according to the LA County registrar's office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They have been given a 48 hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified.

"Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli.

The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including social security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more.

That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county.

California's secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government's demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens.

Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted.

The letters on Friday came on the heels of statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.

data.title: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions remain despite Trump's claims they're lifted
data.description:
Ukraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted

5 hours ago
Hafsa Khaliland
Anastasiia Levchenko,Kyiv

Ukraine is still recording issues with the Starlink internet network, sources within the defence ministry say, after Donald Trump said limits had been reversed by Elon Musk who owns the satellite system.

The sources told the BBC that instances of drones experiencing connection loss at speeds of 161km/h (100mph) were being recorded, hampering military operations.

The US president had denied instructing the tech billionaire to restrict connectivity to Starlink's military-grade counterpart, Starshield, before saying on Thursday that Musk had "put it back".

Asked on Friday, Trump said: "If there is a problem, I will get it straightened out."

Trump added: "I have not spoken to him. I might have to, but I have not. I've heard it was fixed, but if it's not, I'll speak to him."

Musk previously said he was not behind the slowdown, which affected Ukraine's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.

Trump told reporters he did not think the tech billionaire had too much power.

The Ukrainian defence ministry sources said the military was constantly monitoring the performance of both the Starlink and Starshield networks.

They added that there was "currently no confirmation that these restrictions have been lifted".

Last week, Kyiv said uplink speeds to the low Earth orbit satellites had been restricted, affecting the speed at which drones could travel. Any drone travelling faster than 100mph lost its connection, officials said.

Shortly after, Musk said that Starshield, which Ukraine uses for some of its operation, was controlled by the US military and suggested that the Pentagon could be behind the issues.

The White House has since repeatedly denied deliberately placing limits on the network in Ukraine.

In a call with Trump on Friday evening, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham "underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", Downing Street said in a statement.

Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed.

The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.

Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

One Ukrainian soldier said there was "simply no alternative" to Starshield, adding that earlier in the week, connectivity had been cutting out when his unit had been travelling in a car at 80km/h (50 mph).

"I'll tell you this much: God forbid they shut it off completely - it would be an absolute catastrophe," he told the BBC. "We need a backup option for securing communications and internet."

Another soldier said they had reverted to the "proven algorithms" they used before they had Starlink when it initially started playing up, but stressed that Ukrainian forces did need the network, citing its speed.

"Even one or two seconds is critical when we can transfer data and orders faster," she said. "You can really feel that advantage on the battlefield."

Ukrainian reports of a slowdown to the service came during a tense diplomatic row between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky about Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.

While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.

Zelensky said the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump later denied.

The row prompted a war of words between the two world leaders, with Trump suggesting it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and Zelensky implying Trump was not a real leader.

Earlier on Thursday - before Trump's comments - Zelensky had said the speed of the system had still not been restored fully.

"I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."

The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had told Musk that he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped, and that the system was working closer to normal following that conversation.

data.title: 'There's babies in there': Hero dad who stopped Oregon school shooter shares his story
data.description:
U.S.

Hero dad describes taking down Oregon school shooter: "I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams"

By
Lucia I Suarez Sang
Associate Managing Editor
Lucia Suarez Sang is an associate managing editor at CBSNews.com. Previously, Lucia was the director of digital content at FOX61 News in Connecticut and has previously written for outlets including FoxNews.com, Fox News Latino and the Rutland Herald.
Read Full Bio
Lucia I Suarez Sang

Updated on: October 23, 2026 / 4:31 PM EDT / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Kaylub Giamanco, the man praised as a hero for fatally shooting a gunman at a school in Bend, Oregon, last week, is speaking out for the first time about the moments leading up to the shooting and how he is grappling with the aftermath.

The 36-year-old carpenter, whose two daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary School, told Oregon Public Broadcasting that it was happenstance that he was passing by the school at that moment. He said he had decided to go home for lunch that day instead of eating the food he had packed.

As he drove by the elementary school, he saw a "man in black" holding a long gun and shooting at a vehicle. At first, he thought it was a prank, but then the shooter threw the gun over the school fence before climbing it.

"That's when panic fled into my brain and that's when I opened my center console and said, 'No. No. No. No,'" Giamanco said in the interview. In the console of his truck was a .40-caliber handgun he rarely used.

He said he grabbed the weapon's magazine from another compartment, drove into the school parking lot and saw the shooter walk across school grounds.

"I just was in full panic, like, 'No, there's children, there's babies in there,'" he recalled. "I told my Siri to call 911." He said the dispatcher had questions for him, but he didn't stay on the call.

"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,'" Giamanco said.

He described trying to stay out of sight as he followed the gunman.

"I heard him fire two shots into the doors," Giamanco said. "That's when I started hearing children pleading for their lives and then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do."

Giamanco said he crawled in through a broken window, staying on his knees until he reached the special education classroom. He said he saw a teacher struggling with the shooter. He said he swung the door open and fired. 

"He (the shooter) was scrambling for his weapon," Giamanco said. "I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else."

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek was among those who praised Giamanco's bravery, saying he "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." Police Chief Mike Krantz also credited the teacher who tackled the shooter and fought to take his gun, which "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed."

Police later identified the shooter as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II. The attack killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded. 

"I didn't save everybody. I didn't get them all."

After police and first responders arrived at the school, Giamanco went back to his truck, emptied his weapon and called his wife and then his mother.

"She was just like, 'OK, baby, calm down. You did the right thing. You're a hero. You saved lives.' And I was just like, 'I didn't save everybody. I didn't get them all,'" he recalled of the conversation with his mom.

His mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in California, told CBS News Sacramento that her son "has a genuine heart and he loves his community and his family and his children."

A week later, Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting that when he goes to bed at night, he replays that day in his head and wonders if he could have stopped the shooter sooner.

"I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams," he said.

"It was split-second decisions while gunfire was going off, while children were losing their lives."

He grew emotional when talking about the families who lost children.

"I want to apologize for not saving their babies," he said. "The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."

In the days after the shooting, Giamanco sought to avoid the limelight, putting out a brief statement expressing gratitude to first responders and the community. However, he told Oregon Public Broadcasting he's now decided to share his story.

"I've always wanted to change the world, but I've felt small. I'm just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon. I was a nobody other than to my friends and family," he said. "I feel like if I'm going to have a voice, then I'll be damned if I'm not going to use it to change this world, to make it a better place."

He said he hopes to help raise funds for local schools to improve their safety.

data.title: Ramaswamy defends attack ad featuring candidate's estranged mother
data.description:
Vivek Ramaswamy defends ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother

MIKE CATALINI and JULIE CARR SMYTH
Updated Fri, October 23, 2026 at 4:29 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Trump

1 of 2
President Donald Trump listens as gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy speaks at a campaign rally at the Covelli Centre, in Youngstown, Ohio, Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin) (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

Republican Vivek Ramaswamy on Friday defended his campaign's ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton in the closely watched race for Ohio governor.

Speaking at a campaign stop in northeast Ohio, he said the advertisement, which features Acton's mother calling her "a liar," had nothing to do with childhood abuse.

"The irony is they're lying about an ad that is about lying," Ramaswamy said. "They're changing the subject because they don't want to answer for their own failures."

Advertisement

The advertisement features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, criticizing her and insinuating she has mental health issues. Arthur lost custody of her children after her husband, the children's stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton.

Acton is Ohio's former public health director and has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. She has condemned Ramaswamy for the ad.

"I won't normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I'm complaining about." she told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio.

A message seeking comment was sent Friday to her campaign

The ad has stirred significant reaction, including from President Donald Trump, who said it was like "hitting pay dirt."

At a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday, Trump told the crowd Ramaswamy called him to ask for advice.

"You've got to ride with it," Trump recalled telling Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and former presidential candidate. Trump expressed jealousy that he didn't have such a strong ad to run during his own campaigns.

Other Republicans have been critical.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine criticized Ramaswamy and said the ad should be taken down.

"It's wrong to run this ad," DeWine said Thursday.

According to police and court documents obtained by The Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978.

Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty. He was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. He has since died.

data.title: Trump says he ordered the DOJ lawsuit over Alaska race: 'I'm the one that said do it'
data.description:
Trump says he ordered the Justice Department lawsuit over Alaska's US Senate race

NICHOLAS RICCARDI
Updated Fri, October 23, 2026 at 2:46 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Trump

1 of 4
President Donald Trump listens as Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks at a campaign rally at the Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Wasilla, Alaska. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon) (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

President Donald Trump said he told his administration to file a lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president's party is struggling.

"I'm the one that said do it," Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida.

The lawsuit centers on one of the president's longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who Republican fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what's likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state's former congresswoman.

Advertisement

The second Dan Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate.

The lawsuit Thursday by the Republican president's Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. "The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska," the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections.

The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set.

The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state's Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused.

Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary

The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people.

The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice's intervention. "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course," campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. "Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska."

Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses," said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

In a statement on Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska's election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan's campaign was an attempt to "mislead:" voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska's Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot.

"The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters," the DoJ statement said.

The Department of Justice has increasingly been used to bolster the president's political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump's party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the White House race to Democrat Joe Biden.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. "It is not DOJ's intention to, and it's never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed.

The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department.

Constitution gives states the power to run elections

Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. "The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification," Muller said. "The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month."

The U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards set by Congress. That division of power has frustrated Trump, who repeatedly has tried to seize control of election procedures through executive orders that courts have blocked.

The final step for a state election is formally certifying the winner, the act that the administration's lawsuit seeks to prevent, it requests, "pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for. Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."

The process in Alaska is complicated by the state's ranked choice voting system, which Trump opposes, and many expect it to take weeks before a winner is known. Also on the state's ballot is an initiative to repeal that system.

Trump has stepped up complaints about a ballot with dueling Sullivans

Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot, making reference to it during a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week where he called it "CHEATING."

"We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness," the president wrote on Wednesday.

Clogging a ballot with third party candidates to siphon off votes from the other major party is a long-standing tactic in the country's two-party system. Republicans have been linked to an effort to persuade Ohio voters to support a socialist in that state's Senate race, which could help Republican Sen. Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.

___

Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington, DC contributed to this report.

data.title: Ramaswamy's Ohio attack ad prompts debate over what's fair game in politics
data.description:
Ramaswamy's Ohio attack ad shows 'owning the libs' may have limits

Dan Merica, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
Updated Fri, October 23, 2026 at 1:03 AM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump's brand of brash, sometimes offensive, politics has consumed the Republican Party for a decade. But bipartisan outrage over Vivek Ramaswamy's ad featuring his opponent's estranged mother shows how candidates often fail when they try to embody the president's bombast.

Ramaswamy, an Ohio Republican running for governor against Democrat Amy Acton, a former public health official, gained national prominence as the 2024 presidential candidate who sought to mimic Trump's brand of shock-jock politics, confronting his rivals in public and working the sidelines of social media to rile and excite supporters.

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.

Advertisement

Ramaswamy's newest ad features Acton's mother calling her a "liar," even as documents show that Acton and her brother were removed from her home as children after her stepfather was charged with raping Acton.

Political operatives in both parties called the ad an extension of Trump's no-holds-barred politics that catapulted him to the presidency in 2016. Trump's rise was fueled by a Republican ecosystem - much of it online - that has been increasingly shaped in his image over the past decade.

And Trump defended Ramaswamy in an online post on Thursday, calling the ad "very powerful" and writing that criticism is meant only to "damage, demean, and embarrass a Republican."

"I told him leave it up and look upstairs and say 'thank you, God, very much, I appreciate it,'" Trump said at a rally in Iowa on Thursday night, recounting a conversation he said he had with Ramaswamy urging him to keep the ad up.

But the swift bipartisan blowback the ad has received suggests there are limits to the party's attack-first strategy, both now and potentially when Trump eventually steps off the stage in 2028.

Mike DeWine, Ohio's outgoing Republican governor, on Thursday became the latest, and perhaps most significant, figure to denounce the ad, which began airing this week.

"The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," said DeWine, who endorsed Ramaswamy. "It's wrong to run this ad."

That echoed comments made Wednesday by Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican whose reelection campaign is pivotal to his party's hopes of holding on to Senate control. "I would not have run that ad," Husted said.

The string of high-profile denunciations has introduced a level of panic in a red state where Republicans were already concerned with polls showing they could lose critical races.

"The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor," former congressman James B. Renacci, an Ohio Republican who has run for Senate and governor in the state, said in a lengthy overnight post on X Thursday. "And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well."

Criticism of Ramaswamy came from Republicans outside of the state, too.

"It's terrible," Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who is locked in a tight contest for the Senate, told ABC News as she called on Ramaswamy to take the ad down. "I think about it as a mom, and you think about your kid surviving childhood sexual abuse and having to relive that trauma on TV again."

The blowback to Ramaswamy's ad has not been universal.

Ramaswamy has not only defended the spot, but his campaign has pledged to put $4 million behind it. "I would love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans. Unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues," he told reporters earlier this week.

The Ramaswamy campaign decided to put money behind the ads after testing with focus groups showed they were effective, a person briefed on the research told The Washington Post, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy.

Vice President JD Vance, while campaigning in Ohio on Wednesday, said he was "a little bit disgusted" by Republicans who were "whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."

And Shannon Burns, head of one of the state's largest Republican organizations, said the ad has "lit a fuse under a dormant base."

"No matter what the talking heads say or the people who are clutching their pearls say, the Republican base is what matters for Vivek to win," Burns said. "If the Republican base turns out, we win."

Polls show that voters are disheartened by the tone of American politics, including Republicans who have backed Trump. A Gallup survey released late last year found 69 percent of Americans believe the Republican Party and Republicans have gone too far with the use of inflammatory language to attack their opponents, while 60 percent believe the same of Democrats and the Democratic Party.

"Our politics is a reflection of us, and I think that is where we are at as a country, and so our campaigns are reflecting that," said Jason Savage, a longtime Republican operative in Maine who used to run the Maine Republican Party. He argued that too many Republican candidates try "to replicate something they saw before."

"People don't really need you to be Donald Trump," Savage said. "They need you to be you."

This question is particularly potent for Vance, who is openly considering a 2028 campaign and has embraced much of Trump's style.

"Politics is a tough business," Vance said, while publicly reflecting on the ad.

Vance's response angered Republicans who may run against him in 2028.

"Vice President Vance said today that whether this ad by Vivek Ramaswamy was appropriate was not really his concern," Chris Christie, the former governor of New Jersey and a possible 2028 candidate, told The Post. "Seriously?"

Christie added: "Vance's acceptance of this campaign ad only breathes life into the disease that we should be seeking to cure."

Another person formerly close to Trump said the ad was among the clearest examples of the pitfalls of mimicking Trump.

"Trump is an aberration in American politics. So even if it has been successful for him … I am not sure it is readily transferrable to other people," said John Bolton, a longtime Republican figure who served in Trump's first term before breaking with the president.

Because Trump's movement is based more on personality than a set of unifying issues, there is little for his successors to grasp beyond his style, he said.

"There really isn't an -ism to pass on," Bolton said.

Some Republicans argued that Trump's brand of politics often only works when the political environment is behind him. He is now at his lowest ebb in polls, which show deep anger toward Trump over the economy and high gas prices.

In 2016, his bluster met an electorate frustrated by eight years of Democratic control of the White House and the prospect that a second politician from the same family, Hillary Clinton, might become president. In 2024, Trump's constant attacks on President Joe Biden and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris met a restive electorate that felt the Democratic administration was telling them the economy was strong and didn't understand the pain of high prices.

"But the problem unique to this cycle is that nobody cares about a politician having sharp elbows and 'owning the libs' when they can't even afford groceries, a tank of gas and other basic necessities," said a Republican operative involved in multiple races who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak candidly about his party's candidates.

Isaac Arnsdorf contributed to this report.

data.title: Trump admin. seeks to block Alaska Senate result if Dan Sullivan narrowly loses
data.description:
Loading video...
By Giulia Carbonaro

Senior Reporter

Newsweek is a Trust Project member
See more of our trusted coverage when you search.to see more of our trusted coverage when you search.

The Trump administration aims to stop Alaska from certifying the Senate race result if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola and votes for another candidate named Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome.

A lawsuit filed by the Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday against the state of Alaska and various election officials alleges that the Republican candidate listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race intending to mislead voters into backing him instead of the incumbent with the same name.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused Democrats of planting Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, to confuse Alaska voters. In a social media post earlier this week, Trump—who has endorsed the incumbent—called his presence on the ballot a "scam" that could threaten Senator Dan Sullivan's potential victory in what has become one of the closest Senate contests this year.

Read More on News

"Even 1, 2, or 3 percent could make the difference," the president wrote. "Dan S. Sullivan is leading by a lot, but this is CHEATING in an Election, and the Judge that allowed this to happen should be ashamed of himself."

Senator Dan Sullivan is currently 2.7 points behind Peltola, according to VoteHub's poll tracker, underscoring how potentially consequential even a small number of votes could be.

...

Dan J. Sullivan was a member of the Alaska Independence Party until it dissolved late last year, only registering as a Republican when he filed his candidacy in the Senate race earlier this year.

Alaska election officials initially agreed that the retired teacher’s filing was intended to confuse voters and sought to exclude him from the ballot. But an Alaska trial court ruled against that exclusion and the Alaska Supreme Court summarily affirmed that decision, putting Dan J. Sullivan back on the ballot.

The lawsuit hinges on whether the votes cast for the "decoy" Sullivan, a retired teacher, would have changed the winner under Alaska’s ranked choice voting system if they had instead been cast for the Trump-endorsed incumbent.

It would also require an investigation into whether Alaskans who cast their vote for Dan J. Sullivan actually intended to vote for the incumbent, and it would allow further procedures to determine what the election result would have been without the alleged voter confusion.

...

Newsweek contacted the White House, the DOJ, Alaska Division of Elections, Peltola’s and both Sullivans’ campaigns for comment by email on Friday morning, outside of standard working hours.

What Election Experts Think of the DOJ Lawsuit

“The lawsuit is based on very real and valid concerns about voter confusion,” Michael Morley, the Sheila M. McDevitt Professor of Law and Faculty Director of the Election Law Center at the Florida State University, told Newsweek.

“The Alaska secretary of state concluded Daniel J. Sullivan is not an actual good-faith candidate but rather was running only to confuse or mislead voters. Having said that, the DOJ’s lawsuit is completely meritless,” he added.

The DOJ sued under the National Voter Registration Act, Morley said, but does not even allege that the statute has been violated here. “Rather, the DOJ is claiming that allowing the election’s results to be impacted by a sham candidacy would undermine the law’s purpose. That’s not a valid basis for suing,” the professor said.

“Moreover, any concerns about the sham candidacy could have been raised before the election, before votes were cast. Indeed, Alaska courts refused to allow election officials to remove him from the ballot,” Morley added.

The professor believes the lawsuit will be “quickly” dismissed. “If Senator Dan S. Sullivan loses, and Daniel J. Sullivan’s vote tally exceeds the margin of victory, then the senator’s best bet would be to file an election contest with the U.S. Senate, which is the sole judge of its members’ elections and returns. The Senate can decide for itself whether to accept such results.”

Professor Mark Brown, of Capital University School of Law, agrees. “No federal statute authorizes the relief the DOJ seeks and the Alaska Supreme Court has already concluded that Dan J. Sullivan was illegally under Alaska—and federal—law removed from the ballot,” he told Newsweek. “The Alaska Supreme Court thus restored his name to the ballot. DOJ's lawsuit is frivolous.”

Why Are Two Sullivans Running for the Alaska Senate Race?

Six years ago, Alaska narrowly passed a ballot measure shifting the state to a ranked choice voting system allowing voters to rank candidates in order of preference. Ballot Measure 2, which got 50.55 percent of the vote in 2020, created the non-partisan pick one primary and the four-candidate ranked choice voting general election that The Last Frontier is now using.

...

Under this system, which Alaska shares with only one other state in the country, Maine, the top four candidates from each respective primary in the state earlier this year, whether for governor, the House or the Senate, are set to appear on the ballot on November 3, regardless of party affiliation. Voters have the option to rank them in order of preference, though they can also choose one candidate only if they prefer so.

A candidate who receives more than 50 percent of first-choice votes wins outright. If no one passes this threshold, then the candidate who comes in last place is eliminated, and those who selected that candidate first will have their second-choice vote counted. The process continues until one candidate gets more than 50 percent of the vote.

This system is why four candidates are on the ballot in the Alaska Senate race, including Democrat Mary Peltola and Republicans Sen. Dan Sullivan, Dan J. Sullivan Jr., and Gerald Heikes.

The Trump administration, in the DOJ lawsuit filed Thursday, claimed that "the sole purpose of [Dan J. Sullivan’s] candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan."

...

In June, when Dan J. Sullivan was reinstated on the ballot, the retired teacher and fishing enthusiast said that he is running because he is disappointed with Sullivan’s representation and wants change for the state. "It’s a free country," he said, as reported by Courthouse News Service. "Most Alaskans are proud Independents and it’s my sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but ultimately, choice is good and voters’ intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running."

The newly published ballots show that Alaska election officials have come to something of a solution to solve the debate around the two Sullivans. The ballots list incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan as a "Registered Republican" and mark him as the "Incumbent." The retired teacher appears under his full name, "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.," without a party designation displayed beneath his name.

A Key Race for Control of the Senate

Democrats have a chance to seize control of the Senate in the midterms, with Republicans currently holding a narrow 53-47 majority.

While most of the seats up for grabs in the upper chamber are in states where Trump has won by comfortable margins in 2024, the unpopular war in Iran and rising inflation in recent months have turned many of these races into unexpectedly competitive ones.

Alaska, a state which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, has now become a key battleground in the fight for control of the upper chamber, with Peltola gaining ground over the Republican incumbent.

Building on voters’ growing anger over higher prices, Peltola—an Alaskan who supports oil, gas and gun rights—has focused her campaign on the cost of living, trying to appeal to moderate Republicans disappointed with the Trump administration and independents as well as Democrats. Polls show that her strategy may be working.

Who Is Leading the Latest Polls?

With less than two weeks ahead of Election Day, every poll released this month gives Peltola a narrow but consistent lead over Sullivan, while the other two candidates typically receive less than 5 percent of the vote in the first round.

A poll released by progressive pollster Data for Progress earlier this month and conducted between October 8 and October 16 among 675 likely voters, gives Peltola ahead with 49 percent of the vote while Sullivan had 46 percent of the vote in the first round of the election. Dan J. Sullivan had 4 percent of the vote and Heikes only 1 percent. In the final round, Peltola’s lead had grown to 51 percent to Sullivan’s 49 percent. The poll had a margin of error of ±4 percentage points.

...

The Democratic candidate received 48 percent of the vote in an InsiderAdvantage poll conducted between October 9 and October 10, while Sullivan had 43 percent of the vote in a four-way ballot. Dan J. Sullivan Jr. and Heikes received 1.7 percent and 2.2 percent of the vote, respectively, while 5.3 percent of likely voters were undecided.

In the second round of voting, without Dan J. Sullivan and Heikes, 50.1 percent of the vote went to Peltola and 48.0 percent to the incumbent. The poll was conducted among 1,200 likely voters and had margin of error of ±2.83 percentage points.

Americans Want Trump to Accept Outcome of Midterms

A new YouGov survey shows that an overwhelming majority of Americans want the president and his administration to accept the outcome of the midterm elections, no matter the result. According to the poll, conducted on October 22, 2026, among 8,694 U.S. adults, 71 percent of Americans think Trump should "accept the results" if Republicans lose their majority in the U.S. House.

The opinion is bipartisan: 87 percent of Democrats, 67 percent of Independents, and 61 percent of Republicans said the same. Only 8 percent of all voters said Trump should not accept the results, while 21 percent said they were not sure.

YouGov has not released a similar poll on the Senate.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton, Trevor Davies and Emma Lee-Sang

Update 10/23/26, 10:18 a.m. ET: This article was updated with comment from Michael Morley and Mark Brown.

data.title: Blanche says DOJ could block election certification in 'doomsday scenario'
data.description:
Justice Department

Blanche won’t rule out DOJ post-election action in a ‘doomsday’ scenario

The attorney general’s comments come in the middle of a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what election experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizens.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Oct. 22, 2026, 1:38 PM EDT / Updated Oct. 22, 2026, 3:34 PM EDT
By Ryan J. Reilly and Jane C. Timm

NORFOLK, Va. — Attorney General Todd Blanche on Thursday left open the possibility that the Justice Department could seek to block states from certifying votes in the midterm elections, though he said it wasn’t his intention to “improperly interfere with elections.”

NBC News reported this week that the Justice Department is weighing more election-related litigation against states after it sued California to compel state officials to review 18,000 registered voters it suspected could be noncitizens seeking to cast fraudulent ballots. California has an all-mail election and sends out ballots automatically.

01:14

Blanche does not rule out DOJ post-election action

00:0000:00

Washington, D.C., and seven other states do, too: Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington. Mail voting has frequently been a target for President Donald Trump’s voter fraud claims, which have escalated ahead of the 2026 midterms, even as he uses the voting method to cast his ballot in Florida.

On Thursday, Blanche was asked whether he could rule out any action by the Justice Department that could seek to delay the counting of ballots.

Blanche said there could be some “doomsday” scenario in which it would seek to get involved.

“It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process,” he told reporters before he boarded a plane.

Blanche’s comments come in the middle of a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what voting experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizens.

The Justice Department’s role in U.S. elections is limited by law, chiefly allowing it to safeguard civil rights and prosecute people who violate election law.

While private citizens and candidates can sue to challenge ballots or election results, no U.S. laws say the Justice Department can challenge ballots or delay certification. U.S. elections are run by state and local officials, who are charged with certifying results.

Blanche said he couldn’t say there were zero circumstances under which the Justice Department wouldn’t get involved. “Of course, I’m not going to say that,” he said. “But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not.”

Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel traveled to Norfolk for a news conference Thursday to announce racketeering charges against an 82-year-old Virginia state senator.

At that news conference, when he was pressed about the Justice Department’s litigation against states, Blanche said the Justice Department was “not trying to create chaos.” He said it was trying to alert officials to potential issues.

“I’m not trying to not have an election certified. Of course not,” Blanche said. “What we’re trying to do is guarantee to the American people that the only people that are voting are people that are eligible to vote.”

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., reacted to Blanche’s comments, saying Senate Democrats “have been preparing for this for months and will be ready for whatever” the Trump administration tries.

“As Trump and his cronies attempt to steal this election, we are fighting them at every turn,” Schumer posted on X. “Our elections must always belong to the voters — not Donald Trump.”

data.title: Trump says Starlink access restored. Ukraine is reporting more interruptions.
data.description:
Trump says Starlink access restored, but Ukraine reports more interruptions

Victoria Craw and Anastacia Galouchka, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
Updated Fri, October 23, 2026 at 11:01 AM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump said Elon Musk has lifted restrictions on Ukraine's access to Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, amid confusion over who previously ordered access to the network be curtailed.

Trump declined to comment on reports that he called the SpaceX chief executive to ask Ukraine's access to the satellite network be fully reinstated, but described his relationship with Musk as "a very good one." The "bottom line" was that Musk had "put it back," he said in comments to reporters on Thursday.

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.

Advertisement

However, Ukrainian soldiers said Friday they were still experiencing Starshield disruptions, with no indication that any restrictions had been lifted.

On Friday, Starshield was still operating "with constant interruptions," although at a higher speed than on Thursday, Ukrainian commander Andriy "Klima" Klymenko, commander of the 414th Unmanned Systems Brigade, told The Washington Post.

"Right now we don't notice that restrictions on Starlink have been lifted," Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine's defense ministry, wrote in a statement.

Ukraine's military access to Starshield, a secure satellite network designed for government use, was unexpectedly throttled last week, impeding Ukraine's midrange strike campaign on Russian-occupied territory. There is confusion over who ordered access to the network be curtailed, with both Musk and Trump suggesting it was the other side.

The curtailed service followed Trump's announcement of a diesel deal with Russia and demands that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he sought to address high energy prices ahead of the midterm elections.

The Trump administration has faced repeated questions over why access to Starshield was curtailed and who ordered it. The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Musk ordered the slowdown and Trump called him to ask it be lifted.

The White House and Musk did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment.

Trump has recently increased pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to make a deal to end Russia's war against Ukraine, called for his ouster and waived punishing sanctions against Moscow.

Earlier this week, Russia agreed to start restart trilateral talks with Ukrainian representatives, following a meeting between U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. On Friday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said talks were planned for the first half of November, in Abu Dhabi.

On Thursday, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), the senior Democrat on the Senate's permanent subcommittee on ​investigations, said he had opened an inquiry into the restrictions to Starshield services.

In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Blumenthal said it raises questions about who has the technical and legal authority to make such changes and whether the U.S. military had sufficient alternatives if SpaceX-provided services became unavailable.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said Thursday that "innocent Ukrainians have bore the murderous brunt," of limited access to the technology.

"We've spent that week trying to determine the party responsible, but they have yet to own the decision, if in fact one was made," he said. "I have full confidence in the powers of the United States Government and SpaceX to solve this, if there are indeed no objections."

Vice President JD Vance said Thursday it was "completely understandable" that Musk did not want to get involved in the war as he runs a private company.

"I don't think this is about Elon. I think it's fundamentally, what is America's policy in Ukraine and Russia going to be," Vance said.

data.title: Melania Trump secures ceasefire in Russian-held Ukrainian city, White House says
data.description:
Russia, Ukraine agree to Oleshky ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump, White House says

By Steve Holland and Ryan Patrick Jones
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 1:56 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

FILE PHOTO: Drone footage shows destruction in the Russian occupied city of Oleshky

1 of 2
FILE PHOTO: A still image taken from an undated drone video released September 24, 2026, shows destroyed vehicles sitting on a street in Oleshky, Kherson Region, Russian-controlled Ukraine. 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/Handout via REUTERS

By Steve Holland and Ryan Patrick Jones

WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US first lady Melania Trump has secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled city ‌of Oleshky, which will begin on October 29, the White House said on Friday.

Residents of ‌the southern Ukrainian town, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening food crisis.

"Both nations agreed ​to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," a White House statement said.

Advertisement

The development comes as Melania Trump's husband, President Donald Trump, pressures Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to reach an agreement with Russian ‌President Vladimir Putin to end the ⁠war, which began when Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

Melania Trump has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the ⁠war returned to their families.

"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, ​medicine, ​food, and clean water," Melania Trump said in the ​statement.

The ceasefire will allow non-military teams from ‌both countries to visit residents in their homes and coordinate transportation for those wishing to evacuate to either Russia or Ukraine, with an unnamed American media organization accompanying the teams to document the process, the first lady said.

Newsmax, a right-leaning news outlet, said in a report that its cameras would be granted "exclusive access to document the effort."

Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, has ‌a remaining population of 1,700 to 2,000 people — primarily ​elderly residents, along with about 50 children — down from ​roughly 24,000 before the war, the White ​House said. About 90% of the city was flooded following the destruction of ‌the Kakhovka Dam, according to the White ​House.

The statement said Melania ​Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to ​their preferred destination. I anticipate ‌some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.

(Reporting ​by Steve Holland and Susan Heavey; Writing by Ryan Patrick Jones in Toronto; Editing ​by Katharine Jackson, David Ljunggren and Caitlin Webber)
